title: ser vs estar
tagline: Both mean 'to be' — but ser is identity, estar is state. The rule about permanent vs temporary will get you in trouble.

sides.core: Ser encodes what something fundamentally is — identity, category, origin, material.

examples.en: He's boring (as a person).
examples.note: His personality. Swap to está and he's just bored right now — totally different verdict.

examples.es: La boda es en la iglesia.
examples.en: The wedding is at the church.
examples.note: Location of an event uses ser, not estar. Catches everyone out.

examples.en: She's beautiful.
examples.note: Appearance as identity. But 'está muy guapa hoy' means she looks great today — she made an effort.

sides.core: Estar encodes current state — how something is right now, not what it is.

examples.en: He's dead.
examples.note: Death is permanent but it's still a state the body is in. 'Es muerto' doesn't exist.

examples.en: This coffee is really good.
examples.note: Quality you're experiencing right now. 'Es bueno' is a general verdict; 'está bueno' is tasting it.

examples.en: He's ready.
examples.note: Versus 'es listo' = he's clever. Same adjective, completely different meaning depending on verb.

tricky: Adjectives that flip meaning: listo (clever/ready), malo (bad/sick), bueno (good/tasty), vivo (sharp/alive), seguro (safe/certain).

title: fue vs era
tagline: Both are past tense of ser — fue is a completed snapshot, era is the background scenery.

sides.core: Preterite — the event happened, it's done, you're delivering a verdict on it.

examples.en: It was an incredible night.
examples.note: The night is over. You're wrapping it up. Preterite = closing the bracket.

examples.en: He was my best friend.
examples.note: That friendship has ended — he moved away, you fell out, or he died. Fue signals it's finished.

examples.en: How did the interview go?
examples.note: Asking for an overall verdict on a completed event.

sides.core: Imperfect — ongoing background state, what was true across a whole period.

examples.es: Cuando era niño, era muy tímido.
examples.en: When I was a child, I was very shy.
examples.note: No specific moment — a quality that lasted across years of childhood.

examples.es: Era un día tranquilo cuando llegó la noticia.
examples.en: It was a quiet day when the news arrived.
examples.note: Era sets the atmosphere; llegó (preterite) is the event that cut through it.

examples.en: He was my friend (back then).
examples.note: Just remembering a time — no implication the friendship ended badly. Compare fue mi amigo.

tricky: 'Fue' vs 'era' with the same sentence changes meaning: 'fue mi amigo' (friendship ended) vs 'era mi amigo' (fond memory of a time). Native speakers feel this immediately.

title: por vs para
tagline: Para points forward to a goal or recipient. Por looks back at cause, exchange, or movement through.

sides.core: Destination, purpose, recipient, deadline, or a surprising contrast given the subject.

examples.en: I did it for you (you'll benefit).
examples.note: The action is aimed at you as its destination. Compare: 'lo hice por ti' = because of you / for your sake.

examples.es: Para ser extranjero, hablas muy bien.
examples.en: For a foreigner, you speak really well.
examples.note: Sets up a contrast — given what you are, this is unexpected. A sideways compliment.

examples.en: I need it by Monday.
examples.note: Monday is the deadline — the destination in time. Por lunes would mean 'around Monday.'

sides.core: Cause, exchange, duration, movement through space, or on behalf of.

examples.en: I did it because of you / for your sake.
examples.note: You're the reason, not the recipient. The motivation, not the destination.

examples.en: We walked along the beach.
examples.note: Movement through or along. Para la playa would mean you were heading to the beach as a destination.

examples.en: I was ill for a week.
examples.note: Duration. How long the state lasted. Para una semana would imply a deadline.

tricky: 'Gracias por todo' uses por (exchange — you're acknowledging what they gave). Never 'gracias para.' And 'por' in passive voice: 'fue escrito por Cervantes' = written by Cervantes.

title: saber vs conocer
tagline: Saber is knowing facts and skills. Conocer is familiarity through experience — people, places, things you've encountered.

sides.core: Knowing information, knowing how to do something, or knowing a fact.

examples.en: I know how to speak Spanish.
examples.note: Ability or skill always uses saber. 'Conozco hablar' simply doesn't work.

examples.en: Do you know where the pharmacy is?
examples.note: A piece of information — its location. Conocer would mean you've personally visited it.

examples.en: I don't know what to tell you.
examples.note: Knowing what to say = information/ability. Natural and very common.

sides.core: Personal familiarity — you've been there, met them, experienced it firsthand.

examples.en: I know Madrid really well.
examples.note: You've lived there, walked its streets. Not information about Madrid — the city itself through experience.

examples.en: Have you come across this book?
examples.note: You can 'conocer' a book — it means you've encountered it. Not the same as knowing its contents (saber).

examples.en: I don't know her in person.
examples.note: Meeting someone personally = conocer. 'Sé quién es' means I know who she is — just information.

tricky: 'Sé que es famoso' (I know he's famous — a fact) vs 'lo conozco' (I know him — we've met). The distinction maps cleanly to French savoir/connaître or German wissen/kennen.

title: salir vs quedar
tagline: Quedar is making the plan to meet. Salir is the activity of going out. You can have one without the other.

sides.core: Going out — leaving the house, doing an activity, or dating someone.

examples.en: I went out with my friends last night.
examples.note: The activity — you went somewhere together. The evening happened.

examples.en: Are you seeing someone? / Are you dating anyone?
examples.note: 'Salir con alguien' also means to date. Context usually makes it clear, but worth knowing.

examples.es: No me apetece salir esta noche.
examples.en: I don't feel like going out tonight.
examples.note: Salir = leaving the house. Quedar could still happen at home.

sides.core: Arranging to meet — the plan, the agreement, the arrangement. Common in Spain.

examples.en: Shall we meet up Friday? / Are we on for Friday?
examples.note: The arrangement itself. You could then go anywhere. Quedar is the plan, not the outing.

examples.es: Quedé con ella pero al final no salimos.
examples.en: We arranged to meet but we didn't end up going out.
examples.note: Quedar (plan) without salir (activity). They're two separate things.

examples.es: Quedamos en el bar de siempre.
examples.en: We arranged to meet at the usual bar.
examples.note: Quedar + en = where you're meeting. Very natural, very common in Spain.

tricky: In Latin America, 'quedar' for arranging to meet is less common — they'd say 'juntarse' or 'encontrarse.' If you're in Mexico saying '¿quedamos?' people might look confused.

title: llevar vs hacer (time)
tagline: Both express how long something has been going on — but they're built differently and can't be swapped.

sides.core: How long you've been doing something continuously — built into the verb itself.

examples.en: I've been living here for three years.
examples.note: Llevar + time + gerund. The ongoing action is baked in. Elegant and very Spanish.

examples.en: I'd been waiting for two hours.
examples.note: Imperfect of llevar for past ongoing. Works exactly the same way.

examples.en: How long have you been learning Spanish?
examples.note: The natural way to ask. 'Hace cuánto' also works but this sounds more fluent.

sides.core: Hace + time + que — how long ago something started, or how long since something happened.

examples.es: Hace tres años que vivo aquí.
examples.en: I've been living here for three years.
examples.note: Same meaning as the llevar version but different structure. Both are correct; llevar feels more natural in speech.

examples.es: Hace dos horas que te espero.
examples.en: I've been waiting for you for two hours.
examples.note: Emphasis on duration from the speaker's point of view. Slightly more dramatic than llevar.

examples.es: Hacía mucho que no te veía.
examples.en: It had been a long time since I'd seen you.
examples.note: Imperfect hacer for past context. Common opener after a long absence.

tricky: English speakers often try 'estoy viviendo aquí por tres años' — wrong on two counts. Spanish doesn't use present continuous for ongoing duration, and por isn't used this way. Use llevar or hace.

title: pedir vs preguntar
tagline: Preguntar is asking a question. Pedir is asking for something — a request, an order, a demand.

sides.core: To request, to order, to ask for something — you want something from someone.

examples.en: He ordered a white coffee.
examples.note: Ordering food and drink is always pedir. Never preguntar.

examples.en: I'm asking you to listen to me.
examples.note: Pedir + que + subjunctive for making requests of people.

examples.en: He apologised to me.
examples.note: 'Pedir perdón' = to apologise. A fixed phrase — you're requesting forgiveness.

sides.core: To ask a question — you want information, not a thing.

examples.en: She asked me what my name was.
examples.note: Seeking information. Preguntar + indirect question.

examples.es: Pregúntale a él, yo no sé.
examples.en: Ask him, I don't know.
examples.note: Directing someone to ask elsewhere. Always preguntar for questions.

examples.en: I wonder if he'll come.
examples.note: Preguntarse = to wonder. A reflexive use that English speakers often miss.

tricky: 'Ask him for the bill' = 'pídele la cuenta' (request). 'Ask him what time it is' = 'pregúntale qué hora es' (question). The English verb 'ask' covers both — Spanish doesn't.

title: poder vs saber (can)
tagline: Both translate as 'can' — but poder is physical ability or permission, saber is knowing how.

sides.core: Can in the sense of being able to, being allowed to, or it being possible.

examples.en: I can't come tomorrow.
examples.note: Circumstantial — you're busy, unwell, not permitted. Not about skill.

examples.en: Can you smoke here? / Is smoking allowed?
examples.note: Impersonal poder for permission. Very natural way to ask if something is allowed.

examples.en: Could be. / Maybe.
examples.note: One of the most useful phrases in Spanish. Possibility, not ability.

sides.core: Can in the sense of knowing how — a skill you've learned.

examples.en: I can't swim.
examples.note: You never learned. Poder here would mean you're physically prevented from swimming right now.

examples.en: Can you drive? / Do you know how to drive?
examples.note: Skill. Poder conduces would mean 'are you allowed to drive' or 'are you in a state to drive.'

examples.es: De pequeña sabía tocar el piano.
examples.en: When she was little she could play piano.
examples.note: Past ability/skill. Podía here would imply she was allowed or physically capable — different meaning.

tricky: '¿Puedes tocar el piano?' = Are you able to right now / are you allowed to? '¿Sabes tocar el piano?' = Do you know how? The question you mean to ask is almost always saber.

title: deber vs tener que
tagline: Both mean 'must' or 'have to' — deber is moral obligation, tener que is practical necessity.

sides.core: Moral duty, obligation you owe — what you should do as a matter of principle.

examples.en: You must be honest.
examples.note: Moral imperative. Tener que ser honesto would sound more like a practical requirement.

examples.en: I should call her.
examples.note: Conditional of deber = should. The most natural way to express mild obligation in Spanish.

examples.en: I must be right. / I'm probably right.
examples.note: 'Deber de' (with de) = probability, not obligation. 'Debo tener razón' = I have a duty to be right. Huge difference.

sides.core: Practical necessity — you have to do it because of circumstances.

examples.es: Tengo que irme, el tren sale en diez minutos.
examples.en: I have to go, the train leaves in ten minutes.
examples.note: External circumstance forcing the action. No moral dimension — just logistics.

examples.en: You have to try this wine.
examples.note: Strong recommendation. Tener que is common for this in everyday speech.

examples.en: I had to lie.
examples.note: Circumstances left no choice. Debí mentir would sound like you had a duty to lie — odd.

tricky: 'Deber de + infinitive' (deduction: 'must be') vs 'deber + infinitive' (obligation: 'must do'). The tiny 'de' changes everything. 'Debe de estar cansado' = he must be tired. 'Debe estar aquí' = he's supposed to be here.

title: ir vs venir
tagline: Spanish anchors movement to where the speaker is right now — the opposite of English more often than you'd think.

sides.core: To go — movement away from the current location of the speaker.

examples.en: I'm going to the market.
examples.note: Speaker is leaving from where they are. Standard use.

examples.en: I'm coming! / Coming!
examples.note: Spanish says 'I'm going' even when English says 'coming.' Because you're moving away from where you currently are toward them.

examples.es: Fueron a Barcelona el verano pasado.
examples.en: They went to Barcelona last summer.
examples.note: Movement to somewhere away from the reference point — even in the past.

sides.core: To come — movement toward the speaker's current location.

examples.en: Are you coming to the party?
examples.note: The speaker is at (or going to) the party. They're inviting you to join where they'll be.

examples.en: Come here.
examples.note: Movement toward the speaker. The most basic use.

examples.en: I'm coming from work.
examples.note: Venir de = coming from somewhere. The movement ends at the speaker's current position.

tricky: On the phone: '¿Puedes venir?' (Can you come here — to where I am?) vs '¿Puedo ir?' (Can I come — to where you are?). The English verb 'ask' covers both.
